title: Why does the pirarucu drown if it can’t reach the surface?
hook: A fish that can drown. Literally.
summary: The adult pirarucu breathes air with a swim bladder that works like a lung, so it must come to the surface from time to time.

cardBlocks.text: The pirarucu, also called arapaima, is one of the world’s largest freshwater fish and, strange as it sounds, it can drown. As a youngster it breathes with gills. After a certain age, the gills stop developing and gradually lose their function, while the swim bladder, an organ fish normally use to float, turns into something like a lung.

That makes the pirarucu an obligate air-breather: it has to come up to the surface from time to time to fill its bladder with air, roughly every 15 minutes. If it can’t, it doesn’t get enough oxygen from the water. The adaptation lets it live in warm Amazon lakes that are low in oxygen.
The pirarucu breathes air with a swim bladder that became a lung; if it can’t surface, it drowns.

deepDiveBlocks.text: Because the pirarucu has to surface to breathe, fishers in the Mamirauá reserve can count the fish in a lake by watching each rise. Officials use those counts to set how many can be caught.
This strategy can backfire: when oil covers the surface, fish that come up to breathe swallow it and are poisoned. In tests, the pirarucu was the most sensitive species.
